Chapter - 8
Soil Health Management
Dharmendra Kumar, Tapasya Tiwari, Vikas Yadav and Shubha Tripathi
Introduction
Healthy soil is the foundation of agriculture systems that are productive,
productive, and environmentally friendly. Understanding how management
methods affect the soil processes that support plant growth and control
environmental quality can help create a crop and soil management system
that improves and sustains soil health over time. This information should be
read by farmers and gardeners who wish to understand the physical,
chemical, and biological components of good soil and how to manage them. Soil is a valuable resource that may be managed to either improve or
degrade its quality. Plant roots and live bacteria link organic materials and
mineral particles into a dynamic framework that regulates water, air, and
nutrients in the complex ecology that is soil. In an agricultural setting, the
ability of the soil to sustain agricultural productivity and protect
environmental resources is commonly referred to as soil health. The
management of water and air supply, biological control of plant pests, and
nutrient cycling are just a few of the many processes supported by healthy
soil. These functions are influenced by the linked physical, chemical, and
biological properties of soil, many of which are amenable to soil
management strategies. Nutrient Cycling
The word "nutrient cycling" refers to the different procedures through
which nutrients are added to, removed from, and altered in the soil. There are
two main categories of nutrients in soil: organic and inorganic (sometimes
referred to as "mineral"). Organic versions of nutrients have carbon, whereas
inorganic versions do not. Inorganic forms in soil particles, organic forms in
soil organic matter, inorganic forms on cation exchange sites, and dissolved
organic and inorganic forms in the soil solution-the liquid that surrounds soil
particles-are just a few of the ways that the soil stores nutrients.

Page | 90
Where in the Soil are Nutrients Stored? Soil Remedy: Inorganic and a few other types of organic nutrients that
have been dissolved in soil pore water are readily accessible to plants. Cation Exchange Sites: Nutrients with a positive charge are called
cations. Large quantities of macronutrient cations, like calcium, magnesium,
and potassium, are needed by plants. Negatively charged spots on clay and
organic detritus hold onto these positively charged plant nutrients. On cation
exchange sites, plants can instantly get nutrients. The quantity of cation
exchange sites in a specific soil is known as cation exchange capacity
(CEC). Organic Matter: Organic material is made up of living and extinct
organisms in various states of decomposition, such as plant remains and
manure. The type of organic matter and the activity of soil organisms
determine the availability of nutrients to plants during the short to long term. Decomposition is the breakdown of organic matter into simpler organic
and inorganic compounds through processes carried out by soil organisms. Mineralization is the release of plant-available forms of nutrients that
occurs when soil organisms decompose organic matter. Soil Minerals: In the very long run, nutrients in the mineral portion of
soils are made available to plants. The objective of nutrient management for a healthy agricultural soil is to
provide the nutrients necessary for ideal plant growth in the proper quantities
and at the proper times while limiting nutrient losses to the surrounding
environment. Nutrients in the soil can change forms thanks to a variety of nutrient
cycle mechanisms. During several weeks of severe weather in the early
summer, standing water built up in a low part of this field. Denitrification,
which took place while the soil was saturated and nitrogen was lost to the
atmosphere, produced a patch of yellowish, nitrogen-deficient maize. Soil organic matter holds a variety of plant nutrients, such as nitrogen,
phosphorus, and sulfur. Per percentage point of organic matter in the top 6
inches of soil, an acre contains around 1,000 pounds each of nitrogen,
phosphorous, and sulfur. But plants do not readily absorb the majority of the
nutrients found in organic materials. Nutrients in organic matter must be
transformed into inorganic forms by soil organisms through decomposition
and mineralization before they can be utilized by plants.

Page | 91
The soil organic matter was extracted as particles from five different
soils with varying levels of past tillage. Such organic particle matter contains
organic nutrient forms that can be made available to plants through microbial
nutrient degradation mechanisms. The vials on the left had increasing
amounts of tillage in the crop cycle, whereas the vials on the right were
taken from tilled soils beneath permanent grass sod and woods. The vial in
the middle of the field was created on a continuous no-till farm that rotated
its crops every year. Organic matter is broken down by a food web of soil organisms,
releasing nutrients. The base of the food chain organisms, such as bacteria
and fungi, obtain their energy by directly consuming soil organic elements. Plants can use the nitrogen that is released when protozoa and some
nematodes graze on bacteria and fungi. Food Chain in the Soil
In soil, a wide variety of species coexist, and their interactions have a
significant influence on processes that take place above and below ground
(Hooper et al., 2000). The term "soil food web" refers to the group of
organisms that live their entire or part of their lives in the soil. Soil-dwelling
organisms lay the groundwork for important processes such soil structure
development, nutrient cycling and decomposition, bioremediation, and the
promotion of plant health and diversity (Coleman et al., 2004). Organic
matter in soil is the main source of nutrients and energy used by plants and
other living things. Soil organic matter refers to all organic components in or
on the soil, including material derived from plants and animals and in
various stages of degradation. Larger species help to mediate the breakdown of plant and other organic
wastes, such as tiny arthropods, some of which are barely visible to the
human eye. In agricultural environments, common insects and related
species like millipedes, springtails, mites, fly larvae, and burying beetles
actively contribute to decomposition. In addition to helping in the
decomposition of organic materials, decomposers are regularly eaten by
other arthropods (like spiders) and can help keep populations of beneficial
predatory arthropods under check. Nitrogen (N) is a nutrient that can undergo many transformations in the
soil through microbial processes. The process of converting organic nitrogen
to plant-available ammonium (NH4+) is called mineralization. A specific
group of bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate (NO3-) in a process called
nitrification. Nitrogen fixation is carried out by both free-living and root-

Page | 92
symbiotic organisms. Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric
N2 to ammonia (NH3) and is one of the most important ways that nitrogen is
added to the soil ecosystem. In symbiotic nitrogen fixation, nitrogen is fixed
by bacteria within nodules of the roots of plants in the legume family and
ammonia is then taken up by the plant to be turned into an organic form of
nitrogen. The rhizobium/legume symbiosis is the most well-known of the
nitrogen-fixing associations. Legume cover crops will fix more N when
grown in a soil with low NH4+ and NO3-. Soil organic matter contributes significantly to the soil's cation exchange
capacity (CEC), in addition to being a source of nutrients that can be stored. Positively charged nutrients are kept in the soil by cation exchange,
preventing leaching from removing them. One of the few approaches to raise
soil CEC is to increase the organic matter content of the soil. The pH of the soil, which gauges the activity of hydrogen ions (H+) in
the soil solution, has an impact on a variety of aspects of nutrient cycling and
soil biology. Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is alkaline, and pH 7 is regarded as
neutral. Generally speaking, crops thrive in soils with a pH between 6-7,
though there are few outliers. Aluminium in the soil changes form and
becomes poisonous to plant roots as the pH falls below 6. At a low pH of the
soil, manganese can also increase to dangerous levels. Soils in humid areas
of the world will naturally lean towards acidity; therefore, liming agents that
neutralise acidity must be added to maintain soil at an ideal pH. The pH of the soil affects the availability of many micronutrients, with
iron, manganese and zinc becoming increasingly available as pH rises. As
pH grows more alkaline, molybdenum becomes more readily available. The
requirement for a certain micronutrient frequently affects a crop's preference
for a pH outside the typical range of 6-7. The molybdenum-dependent
nitrogen-fixing enzyme requires a soil pH of about 7 for legumes to thrive. Blueberries prefer a pH of 4.5 to 5 because they require a lot of iron. The pH
of the soil also has an impact on soil organisms. Near-neutral soil pH is
preferred by bacteria and earthworms. Fungi thrive at most soil pH levels;
therefore, they frequently predominate the soil microbial population in acidic
soils. The cation exchange capacity provided by organic matter is influenced
by soil pH as well. The cation exchange sites on soil organic matter will
increase when soil pH rises. Pest Organisms are Controlled Biologically
One ecosystem service provided by soil organisms that is especially
important to agricultural systems is the biological control of arthropod pests.

Page | 93
The term "biological control" describes the process of eradicating pest
organisms using their natural enemies, which can include pathogens,
parasites, and predators. Healthy agricultural soil communities typically
contain a range of predators, parasites, and diseases that aid in the
management of agricultural pests. Spiders, harvestmen, and ground (carabid)
beetles are a few noteworthy ground-dwelling natural adversaries of insect
pests. Ground beetles greatly improve the health of agroecosystems by
taking part in the destruction of insects, weed seeds, and slugs. Mycorrhizal Arbuscular Fungi
The beneficial soil organisms known as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungus
support a number of soil health characteristics. Mycorrhizal fungus and plant
roots live together in harmony. Symbiosis is the name for a close coexistence
of various species. The fungus has relatively regular and direct access to the
plant's carbohydrates thanks to this relationship. In return, the plant benefits
from the fungus' ability to penetrate the soil and create hyphae or mycelium,
a network of fungal biomass that resembles threads and considerably widens
the root system. For an extended period of time, mycorrhizal fungi need the host plant as
an energy source. A symbiotic relationship exists between mycorrhizal fungi
and over 80% of land plants. Some notable crops and weeds that are not
mycorrhizal include brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, radish, canola, etc.) and
chenopods (spinach, chard, lambs quarters, etc.). Mycorrhizal fungi are particularly adept at aiding plants in acquiring
phosphorus, a nutrient that is largely immobile in soil. Because plant roots
are immobile, a phosphorus depletion zone develops around them as they
extract phosphorus from the soil. Mycorrhizal fungi act as an extension of
the plant's root system, absorbing phosphorus from non-depleted areas and
transporting it to the root. The outer hyphae of mycorrhizal fungus contribute in soil
agglomeration by secreting glomalin, a material akin to glue. Glomalin helps
soil particles stick together to create aggregates that maintain soil porosity
and prevent erosion. Mycorrhizal symbioses make plants more stress-resistant. Plant diseases
can't infect the roots because of the network of fungi that surrounds them. Mycorrhizal fungi can lessen plant illnesses by enhancing plant nutrition,
enhancing root toughness, altering the chemical composition of plant tissues,
reducing abiotic stress, and altering the microbial population on roots.

Page | 94
Numerous factors affect the populations of mycorrhizal fungus in the
soil. Tillage disrupts the network of delicate fungal strands, which decreases
populations. High quantities of phosphorus in the soil also lower mycorrhizal
populations because phosphorus reduces plants' ability to support the
symbiosis. Last but not least, because mycorrhizal fungi depend on a host
plant for energy, they will eventually become extinct during extended times
without one, such as those found in arid fallow fields or when a nonhost crop
is grown as part of a rotation. The majority of native soils are home to large populations of
mycorrhizal fungi that are active or dormant spores that become active when
a host crop is produced. Soil inoculation with mycorrhizal fungus is typically
not required. Regulation of Air and Water in Soil
Plants require water and oxygen in the root zone for the optimal growth. Both air and water are held in the pore space of soil, which exists between
soil aggregates and soil particles. The diameters of the pores that occur
between and within soil aggregates determine how water and gases enter and
are retained by the soil. Larger holes, also known as macropores, are
essential to provide efficient aeration and fast entry of rainfall. Smaller pores
called micropores are essential for holding and absorbing water. While macropores are frequently visible to the human eye, micropores
between and within microaggregates are not. In order for good plant growth
to occur, the soil has to have both macro-and micropores for optimal aeration
and water supply. The soil on the left is easily crumbled when handled, revealing wellformed macroaggregates and the macropores that connect them. The cloddy
soil on the right only has a few macropores where the soil has burst. The soil
on the right is from a heavily tilled field, whereas the dirt on the left is from
the grass sod next to the same field. The formation of pores in the soil occurs when soil particles cluster
together to form a hierarchy of aggregates. Soil organisms considerably
improve aggregate stability and soil aggregate formation. The "glue" of clay,
organic components, root hairs, organic compounds from bacteria and fungi,
and fungal hyphae holds soil aggregates together. Aggregate stability is the
capacity of soil aggregates to withstand erosive water stresses. Good
aggregate stability supports aeration, discharge from rainfall, soil erosion,
and the preservation of macropores in the soil. Aggregates also help to
conserve soil organic matter because the organic matter they contain is
physically protected from microbial decomposition.

Page | 95
Soil Organic Matter
Utilizing soil organic matter allows for the integration of several aspects
of soil health. It is possible to distinguish between labile and stable pools of
soil organic matter, and each has particular characteristics and functions in
the soil. The proportion of organic matter in agricultural soils can range from
1 to 8 percent, depending on factors like temperature, soil type, and
management techniques. The labile pool of organic matter, which makes up 5-20% of the total
pool of soil organic matter, consists of the living biomass of soil organisms
and plant roots, minute fragments of organic detritus, and relatively simple
organic compounds like polysaccharides, organic acids, and other substances
that are synthesized by microbial activity or are by-products of
decomposition processes. Labile organic material is the primary fuel source
for the soil food web because it is quickly decomposed by bacteria. It is the
principal source of easily mineralized organic nitrogen that is available to
plants. Management Practices to Improve Soil Health
1. Reduce Inversion Tillage and Soil Traffic
Numerous factors contribute to excessive tillage being bad for soil
health. The decomposition of organic matter is a result of tillage, which
increases oxygen levels in the soil and encourages microbial activity. Tillage
also damages soil aggregates, making organic matter particles that had been
structurally protected by aggregates vulnerable to microbial oxidation. Organic matter levels will gradually decrease over time, lowering soil health,
if organic matter additions are insufficient to make up for decomposition
losses. Additionally, crop residues produce less soil coverage due to
inversion tillage, leaving the land more vulnerable to erosion. Management Practices for Good Soil Health
Common Primary Tillage Implements
Moldboard Plow: Inverts the soil to bury residues, terminate cover
crops and perennial sod, and kill weeds. Disk Plow: Concave disks mounted in a gang cut the residue and invert
the soil laterally, allowing the residue to mingle with the soil and loosen it. The size, form and tilt angle of the disks affect soil disturbance and residue
incorporation. Chisel Plow: Without inversion, chisel-pointed curved shanks are
pulled through the ground. Loosens the top layer of soil and incorporates

Page | 96
some waste into it. Chisel point width and twist affect soil disturbance and
residue assimilation. Moldboard plough tillage (photo's left side) inverts the soil, burying
weeds, sod and surface debris. While loosening the soil without inversion,
chisel plowing (right side of photo) keeps residue on the soil's surface. Tillage can also harm the hyphal network of the mycorrhizal fungi,
which may eventually lead to their decline. When inadequately managed, the
majority of inversion and noninversion tillage techniques compact the
subsoil, creating a plough pan that restricts root growth and access to water
and nutrients in the subsoil. Wheels and people can flatten the soil's top layer
if they are used excessively, which reduces microporosity and inhibits root
growth. 1. Compacted Soil
Soil compaction happens when heavy foot and machine traffic is applied
to damp, plastic soil. This traffic reduces pore space and increases bulk
density by compressing the soil. Because macropores are squeezed more
than micropores, there is less water infiltration, less drainage and more
runoff. Soil compaction makes it more challenging for plant roots to sift
through the soil. The reduction in pore space also has an impact on numerous
tiny, incapable of moving soil particles and restricted to the pore space and
channels already existent in the soil. Physical disruptions like inversion tillage have a substantial impact on
the biological features of soil as well. It may be possible to lessen soil
moisture and the amount of space available for soil-dwelling organisms by
removing surface detritus and compaction. Conservation tillage management
may provide a greater variety and quantity of arthropod predators associated
with the soil surface than regular inversion tillage. It may help increase
natural control of pest insects in soil. Beneficial insects related to the soil
have a higher chance of surviving in fields where noninversion tillage (like
chisel plowing) is used. When compared to inversion tillage methods (such
the moldboard plough), noninversion tillage causes less soil disturbance and
hence causes less direct soil organism mortality. 2. Increase Organic Matter Inputs
To maintain or increase soil organic matter levels, inputs of organic
matter must match or exceed losses of organic matter from decomposition. Since healthy crops can be a rich supply of organic matter, it is advisable to
return crop wastes to the soil as much as possible. One can also use cover

Page | 97
crops or perennial plants, compost, animal dung and green manure to
improve or preserve soil organic matter. You can monitor the evolution of
soil organic matter by requesting an organic matter study when sending soil
fertility sample to your soil testing laboratory. Be sure that your organic
matter comparisons over time are based on data from the same lab or from
labs that use the same procedure for organic matter analysis, as results can
differ significantly between analysis methods. 3. Use Cover Crops
Numerous advantages cover crops bring to soil health. They lessen the
chance of erosion by keeping the soil covered throughout the winter and
other seasons when crops are dormant. The biomass created by cover crops
is often transferred back to the soil, increasing the amount of organic matter. Taproot-bearing cover crops can open macropores and reduce compaction. Fibrous-rooted cover crops can aid in soil stabilization and aggregate
development. Mycorrhizal fungi can be maintained and multiplied in
population by species of cover crops that host them. Through nitrogen
fixation, legume cover crops can enrich the soil with nitrogen. Nitrate and
other nutrients that are subject to leaching losses can be retained by cover
crops. 4. Reduce Pesticide Use and Provide Habitat for Beneficial Organisms
The use of broad-spectrum pesticides can harm beneficial insects that
aid in biological control or pest organisms. Farm scaping is an ecological
method used across the entire farm to maintain biodiversity and promote the
presence of beneficial creatures. For the purpose of attracting and supporting
populations of beneficial species including insects, spiders, amphibians,
reptiles, bats, and birds that parasitize or predate on insect pests, farm
scaping techniques include the use of insectary plants, hedgerows, cover
crops, and water reservoirs. The soil is stabilized by farm fences positioned
in ridges between fields, steep ditches, or vulnerable locations. Farm scaping
can also be used as a filter strip to prevent water runoff and soil erosion. Plants used in farms capes contribute to healthy soil by adding organic
matter, the base of the soil food web. 5. Rotate Crops
Crop health will increase as a result of the disruption of soilborne pest
and disease life cycles by diverse crop rotations. Rotations can also help with
weed management. Pests that thrive inside a particular crop are prevented
from having a chance to establish their populations over time by producing a
variety of crops throughout time and area. Crop rotation can also aid in
reducing nutrient surpluses.

Page | 98
6. Manage Nutrients
You can meet crop nutrient needs and reduce nutrient excesses by
carefully managing the timing, application strategy, and quantity of manure,
compost, and other fertilizers. Plants that are strong and able to grow quickly
can resist pest harm better. Overfertilizing crops, though, can exacerbate pest
issues. Plants with increased amounts of soluble nitrogen may become less
pest-resistant, which could lead to higher pest densities and crop damage. It
will be easier to access nutrients and less hazardous to grow crops if the soil
pH is kept at a level that is suitable for the crop. Keeping calcium levels at a
healthy level will promote earthworm growth and enhance soil
agglomeration. Managing Nutrients in Soil
Nitrogen (N) Management
•
Nitrate nitrogen is susceptible to leaching losses because the
negative charge of the molecule is not held by cation exchange sites
of soil particles. Leaching occurs mainly in the fall, winter, and
early spring.
•
Nitrogen in urea-containing fertilizers and manure is susceptible to
volatilization losses as ammonia gas when not incorporated into the
soil.
•
Nitrate nitrogen can be lost to the atmosphere through conversion
into nitrous oxide and nitric oxide gases by microorganisms in
warm, poorly aerated soil.
•
Nitrogen losses can be minimized with appropriate timing and
application of fertilizers and manures and by using cover crops to
limit leaching losses in the winter. Phosphorus (P) Management
•
Phosphorus is tightly bound to soil particles and does not easily
diffuse through the soil.
•
Mycorrhizal fungi can assist plant roots in P acquisition in low-P
soils.
•
Adding organic matter can mask the P binding sites on soil
particles, increasing P availability.
•
Phosphorus can accumulate to excessively high levels when P
inputs in manure and fertilizer exceed P removal by crops; this can
occur in soil that receives annual manure applications at rates to
supply crop nitrogen needs.

Page | 99
•
Erosion can transport soil particles with high levels of P into
waterways where P can become a pollutant.
•
Environmental P pollution can be limited by reducing erosion and
maintaining soil P levels in the optimum range of 30-50 ppm
